clinicalPearls: A triad of asthma, recurrent nasal polyposis with chronic rhinosinusitis and respiratory reactions to aspirin and other non-selective NSAIDs
Ingestion of aspirin or an NSAID provokes upper and lower airway reactions such as rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, bronchospasm and sometimes flushing
The asthma and nasal polyps are typically severe and the polyps recur rapidly after surgery
It usually develops in adulthood and is not a classic IgE-mediated allergy
Diagnosis may be confirmed by a supervised aspirin challenge where the history is unclear
Management includes standard asthma and polyp treatment, avoidance of NSAIDs, and aspirin desensitisation in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease is driven by dysregulation of arachidonic acid metabolism. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase-1 by aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs reduces protective prostaglandin E2 and shifts metabolism toward overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are already elevated at baseline. The resulting eosinophilic inflammation of the upper and lower airways produces severe asthma and nasal polyposis, and NSAID exposure precipitates acute reactions by unmasking this leukotriene excess rather than through an IgE mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps without NSAID sensitivity
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history of respiratory reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs
Assessment of asthma control and sinonasal disease including nasal endoscopy and imaging
Supervised aspirin (or NSAID) challenge in a controlled setting when diagnosis is uncertain
Eosinophil and, where relevant, leukotriene assessment
Exclusion of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
redFlags: Features suggesting eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (neuropathy, vasculitic rash)
Poorly controlled asthma with frequent exacerbations
reference.prognosis: The disease is chronic, but with NSAID avoidance, modern asthma and polyp therapies and aspirin desensitisation in appropriate patients, control is often substantially improved.
pitfalls: Not warning patients to avoid non-selective NSAIDs
Attempting aspirin challenge or desensitisation without appropriate supervision
Missing eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis as a mimic
Undertreating the underlying asthma and rhinosinusitis
management: Strict avoidance of aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs, substituting paracetamol or a selective COX-2 inhibitor when analgesia or anti-inflammatory treatment is needed
Optimised asthma control with inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators
Leukotriene-modifying therapy, using a receptor antagonist such as montelukast or a synthesis inhibitor, targeting the cysteinyl-leukotriene overproduction central to the disease
Nasal polyp and rhinosinusitis treatment with intranasal corticosteroids and endoscopic sinus surgery for refractory or obstructing polyps, recognising their rapid recurrence
Aspirin desensitisation followed by regular aspirin therapy in selected patients to improve sinonasal and asthma control
Biologic therapy such as anti-IL-5, anti-IL-4/13 dupilumab or anti-IgE for severe eosinophilic asthma and polyposis
Exclusion of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, with multidisciplinary respiratory, allergy and ENT follow-up
